When I started, this whole job used to be a filing job. That is the honest description. There used to be a room, an actual room, with the returns in boxes, and two people whose entire year was that room. Nobody used to ask a software company about compliance, because compliance was not something you bought, it was something you employed people to do. What changed was not the technology. The technology had been there for years. What changed was that the regulator tightened the rules and started asking for the trail, and suddenly the question was not can you file it, it was can you prove who touched it. Every company I sell to still has a legacy system somewhere doing something important, and half of them do not know which one it is. That is the conversation now. It did not use to be.

I have been on both sides of this and the thing that surprises people is how fast outdated happens. We were the benchmark. For about six years everybody in our segment compared themselves to us, and then in eighteen months we were the ones lagging behind, and honestly nobody inside the building noticed until a client said it out loud in a meeting. What I would tell anybody is that you do not fall behind by standing still. You fall behind because the rules move while you are doing exactly what worked. They moved the goalposts twice in one year, and the second time we were still building for the first change. The overhaul took two years and it should have taken one, and the reason it took two is that we spent the first six months arguing about whether we needed it.
